name: Philippa 'Pip' Ashdown
languages: German (two years at a college in the East, reading Goethe and arguing)
equipment: Heavy overcoat, camel hair, from her father's tailor, with deep pockets for notebooks
.32 pocket pistol (Colt 1903 hammerless, her grandfather's, engraved), 8 rounds loaded, in the coat pocket
Ledger press card, PRESS hatband card, and a pass to the Hall of Justice pressroom
Three reporter's notebooks, filled with shorthand nobody else can read
A Rolodex card file of every useful telephone number on Larch Hill, in a shoebox in her car
A borrowed Speed Graphic camera with flashbulbs (she is a bad photographer and knows it)
Her grandmother's pearls, which get her into places, and a lipstick that gets her out of them
A key to the Ashdown house on Larch Hill, which she has not used since Easter
Car: 1950 Studebaker Champion convertible, red, a twenty-first birthday present she is ashamed of and loves
features: Doors Open (Old Money origin: doormen, club secretaries and private secretaries let her through unless told not to, and she has advantage on Society checks among the wealthy; below the tracks she has disadvantage on Streetwise until she has spent a scene earning trust)

Press Pass (Reporter: with her press card in her hatband she gets into crime scenes, press boxes, courtrooms, City Hall corridors, hospital lobbies and the coroner's office; a source who talks to her is never burned by her, whatever it costs, and her sources know it)

The Morgue (Reporter: her Research checks take half the usual time, and once per long rest an hour in the Ledger morgue or a call to the city desk gives one fact the paper has printed about a named person, business or address)

Ink by the Barrel (Reporter, 2nd level: when she threatens to print what she knows about someone with a reputation to protect, she can use INT for the Intimidation check and has advantage on it; the threat is remembered)
Beat: Society Page (Reporter, 3rd level: proficiency bonus doubled for Society checks, and she can get herself invited to any party, opening or charity function in the city)
Family Name (Society Heir background: the Ashdown name opens Larch Hill; she knows the hilltop's scandals and is the goddaughter of Cornelius Vantreight, who has known her since the day she was born)

personality.traits: I talk very fast, in long sentences, and I interrupt people because I have usually worked out where they are going. I take notes during conversations, openly, and am surprised when people mind. I swear like a longshoreman and have the manners of a duchess, sometimes in the same sentence.
personality.ideals: The truth is the only thing worth printing and the only thing anybody up on the Hill is afraid of. Print it, and let the lawyers sort it out.
personality.bonds: The Ledger, the poorest, best and most stubborn newspaper on the coast, which gave me a job when my own family thought I was a joke. And Hollis Gage, who is the father I would have chosen.
personality.flaws: I was born on Larch Hill and I am still, under all of it, a little bit sure that the rules are for other people. And I would sell nearly anything, including a friend, for the right front page; I just have not been offered the right one yet.

appearance: A small, quick, fair-haired woman of twenty-nine with a sharp, freckled, clever face, a straight nose she inherited from three generations of bankers, and a smile that makes people tell her things. She dresses expensively and carelessly, in her father's castoffs cut down, a camel coat with ink on the cuffs, and pearls. She smells of cigarettes and Chanel.
backstory: Philippa Ashdown is the youngest daughter of the Ashdowns of Larch Hill (timber, then banking, then nothing in particular), and grew up three doors down from Greyholme, where Cornelius Vantreight, her godfather, gave her a pony on her sixth birthday and a lecture on the dangers of reading too much on her sixteenth. She went East to college, came back with a degree in English and an unsuitable interest in crime, and in 1947 walked into the Ledger and asked Hollis Gage for a job. He gave her the night police beat to get rid of her, and she was so good at it that he made her his crime reporter in 1949. Her family has not forgiven either of them. She met Walt Embry on a murder story in 1950 and has been doing research for the agency in exchange for exclusives ever since. She takes the Sloane job because a DA in fear of his life the week before an election is the story of the year, and because, on Tuesday morning, when she reads the Halvorsen file, she remembers being at Greyholme as a girl when the news of the fire came, and her godfather putting down the telephone and finishing his soup.
